claims.text: Corrosion protection of pre-exposed Q235 steel is governed by the stability and integrity of its native oxide film.
The native oxide film on Q235 steel remains intact during room-temperature aggressive-salt exposure.
At 700–900 °C, enhanced diffusion-induced phase changes destabilize the native oxide on Q235 steel.
At 700–900 °C, oxide spallation destabilizes the native oxide on Q235 steel.
Disruption of the native oxide exposes Q235 steel and accelerates corrosion in high-temperature salt.
As-received Q235 steel has a thin, naturally formed, Fe-rich passivation layer.
Low diffusion rates at room temperature preserve a continuous protective iron oxide containing phases such as Fe3O4.
Increased atomic mobility at high temperature promotes transformation of magnetite into more porous hematite.
Aggressive molten salt can promote dissolution processes that contribute to loss of protection.
Thermal-expansion mismatch causes microcracking and spallation of the Q235 oxide film.
Room-temperature aggressive-salt exposure will produce minimal mass change and leave an intact, adherent oxide film on Q235 steel.
High-temperature salt exposure will cause more oxide disruption and mass loss than room-temperature salt exposure.
Dense surface passivation films can provide good corrosion resistance.
The native oxide on Q235 steel is known to provide passivation at room temperature in inert or non-aggressive environments.
The proposed mechanism applies specifically under oxidizing chloride- or sulfate-based salt conditions.
The proposed mechanism does not apply to engineered coatings, alloy-modified steels, or non-oxidizing environments.
The relative contributions of oxide transformation and mechanical spallation may depend on salt chemistry and exposure duration.
Comparing gravimetry, SEM morphology, XRD phase composition, and oxide adhesion after room- and high-temperature exposures can test the proposed mechanism.
